notes.short: Desire conceives and gives birth to sin
notes.about: Desire is pictured as a woman who conceives and gives birth to sin; and sin, once full-grown, gives birth to death. The picture shows that sin starts in a person's own desire, not from God (verse 13), and grows until it ends in death.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death
figure.means: sin starts when a person's own desire is given its way, and it grows until it ends in death

original.note: In Greek the verbs are those of childbearing: one for conceiving and two for giving birth, the second used of sin bringing forth death.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Personification, human actions given to things. Albert Barnes says the allusion is obvious: when desire is acted on, sin is produced, so sin is not to be traced to God. Adam Clarke says the Greek verbs show the figure of conceiving and bringing forth. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) pictures desire as a harlot who brings forth sin.
notes.limit: Not all the writers name the figure, and one calls it a metaphor; they agree on what it shows.

cites.at: Prosopopoeia: human actions given to things, p. 869
cites.quote: “When lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin.” See under Climax.

cites.quote: The allusion here is obvious. The meaning is, when the desire which we have naturally is quickened, or made to act, the result is that sin is produced. … The design of all this is to show that sin is not to be traced to God, but to man himself … The result of sin when it is fully carried out, is death

cites.quote: When the evil propensity works unchecked, it bringeth forth sin - the evil act between the parties is perpetrated. … Any person acquainted with the import of the verbs συλλαμβανειν, τικτειν , and αποκυειν, will see that this is the metaphor, and that I have not exhausted it.

cites.quote: The guilty union is committed by the will embracing the temptress. "Lust," the harlot, then, "brings forth sin," namely, of that kind to which the temptation inclines.
